title: Heavy rain cools Delhi, causes traffic snarls, waterlogging; yellow alert issued for Friday - ThePrint

full_text:
New Delhi, Aug 6 (PTI) Heavy rain lashed several parts of Delhi on Thursday, inundating roads, triggering widespread traffic snarls and waterlogging, and bringing a sharp drop in temperatures across the national capital.
With heavy rainfall, Thursday became Delhi’s wettest day of August so far this year, offering respite from the humidity.
According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Lodi Road recorded the highest rainfall between 8.30 am and 5.30 pm at 60.4 mm, followed by Safdarjung at 56.0 mm, Ridge at 54.4 mm, Ayanagar at 22.3 mm and Palam at 14.6 mm.
The cumulative rainfall recorded since 8.30 am stood at 43.8 mm at Lodi Road, 25.2 mm at Palam, 18.7 mm at Safdarjung, 17.2 mm at Ridge and 14.2 mm at Ayanagar, the IMD said.
The rainfall brought down the maximum temperature significantly across the city. Safdarjung recorded a maximum of 27.6 degrees Celsius, 6.6 notches below normal. Lodi Road recorded 27.8 degrees Celsius, 5.2 notches below normal; Palam 27.3 degrees Celsius, 7.1 notches below normal; Ridge 27.6 degrees Celsius, 6.4 notches below normal and Ayanagar 27.2 degrees Celsius, 6.8 notches below normal.
Minimum temperatures also remained below normal. Safdarjung recorded 25.6 degrees Celsius, 1.3 notches below normal; Lodi Road 25.4 degrees Celsius, 0.6 notch below normal; Ayanagar 25.2 degrees Celsius, 1.2 notches below normal; Palam 23.2 degrees Celsius, 3.6 notches below normal; and Ridge 22.5 degrees Celsius, 3.7 notches below normal.
The weather office has forecast a generally cloudy sky with heavy rain on Friday and issued a yellow alert for the national capital. Sangam Vihar was among the worst-hit areas, with roads submerged and traffic movement severely disrupted. Waterlogging was also reported from Sainik Farms, Shastri Park, Rohtak Road, Tughlaqabad, near the Red Fort and parts of ITO, where inundated roads brought vehicles to a crawl.
Heavy congestion was reported from several key arterial roads, including Aruna Asaf Ali Marg, Shaheed Jeet Singh Marg, Ber Sarai, the JNU Gate-Jia Sarai stretch, NH-48 between Dhaula Kuan and Rajokri flyover towards Gurugram, MB Road, Kalindi Kunj, Najafgarh, Rajdhani Park-Mundka, the ITO-Laxmi Nagar stretch, Akshardham, the CWG Village-Nizamuddin Bridge-Sarai Kale Khan corridor and the Delhi-Dehradun Expressway.
Mahesh Palawat, vice president (Meteorology and Climate Change) at Skymet Weather, said Delhi and adjoining areas are likely to receive moderate rain over the next two to three days under the influence of multiple weather systems.
He said a western disturbance over the Himalayas, cyclonic circulations over Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and the Darjeeling region, an active monsoon trough and enhanced moisture incursion from the Bay of Bengal are expected to keep rainfall activity over north India active.
According to Palawat, the systems are likely to bring widespread rainfall across the Indo-Gangetic plains, with heavy rainfall likely in some areas. Delhi is expected to receive light to moderate rain till August 10, although isolated pockets may witness intense showers.
Meanwhile, the city’s air quality was recorded in the “satisfactory” category at 4 pm, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 74, according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).
According to the CPCB, an AQI between zero and 50 is considered “good”, 51 to 100 “satisfactory”, 101 to 200 “moderate”, 201 to 300 “poor”, 301 to 400 “very poor”, and 401 to 500 “severe”. PTI SGV MPL MPL

The flash flood-affected regions in Kerala are likely to witness intensified rainfall over the next two days under the combined influence of cyclonic circulations over the Bay of Bengal. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert on Thursday (August 6, 2026) warning of extreme heavy rainfall in Pathanamthitta, Idukki and Kottayam districts, and an orange alert for Kollam, Alappuzha, Ernakulam, Kannur and Kasaragod districts, where very heavy rainfall is likely.
A yellow alert has been issued for the remaining six districts, warning of isolated heavy rains for the day.

Swell waves

ROME, Aug. 6 (Xinhua) -- Italy on Thursday placed all 27 major cities monitored by the Health Ministry under the highest-level red alert for extreme heat for the first time since the country's heat warning system was introduced, as the fourth heatwave of the year continued to grip the country, according to Italy's ANSA news agency.
The latest red alerts were extended to the southern cities of Messina and Reggio Calabria, bringing the total number of cities under the maximum warning level to 27.
Weather forecasters said the current spell of scorching temperatures is expected to persist for at least another 10 days, with temperatures reaching around 40 degrees Celsius in parts of the country.
The Health Ministry's Level 3 red alert indicates a heatwave emergency characterized by prolonged high temperatures that pose health risks not only to vulnerable groups, but also to healthy people.
According to forecasts, the northern city of Bolzano is expected to see its warning level downgraded to orange on Friday, while the remaining cities are likely to stay under red alert.
Italy has experienced four major heatwaves so far this summer. The prolonged heat, together with drought and wildfires, has been linked to a number of deaths and disrupted economic activities, particularly in the agricultural sector.
Around 70,000 hectares have burned in Italy because of wildfires so far this summer, an area equivalent to roughly 100,000 soccer fields, the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) said in a report on Wednesday.
Scientists were quoted by Ansa as saying that climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, including heatwaves, droughts, severe storms and flooding, making such events more common across the Mediterranean region.■

title: Serbia fights raging wildfires amid severe heat and drought - The Assam Tribune
full_text:
Belgrade, Aug 6: Serbian emergency services are battling multiple wildfires across the country as strong winds, extreme heat and prolonged drought intensify fire conditions, with a reignited blaze in the Deliblato Sands protected nature reserve in northeastern Serbia burning around 300 hectares of pine forest.
Serbia's public broadcaster RTS on Wednesday (local time) reported that a fire extinguished in the Deliblato Sands about 10 days ago flared up again after ground-level embers were fanned by strong winds.
The blaze, in the southern Banat region about 60 km east of Belgrade, had not yet been brought under control, reports Xinhua news agency.
Serbian Interior Ministry said it had committed all available personnel and equipment. According to RTS, 45 firefighters from several towns, volunteer fire brigades and three police helicopters were tackling the fire, while no buildings were under threat.
Meanwhile, emergency services continued to battle several other fires across the country.
The wildfires coincide with the peak of a prolonged heatwave. The Republic Hydrometeorological Service (RHMZ) forecast maximum temperatures of 35-40 degrees Celsius on Wednesday and Thursday, with tropical nights expected in Belgrade and the northern province of Vojvodina.
The prolonged drought has also lowered river levels across Serbia. RHMZ warned that the Danube, Sava and Tisa rivers are expected to remain below navigational thresholds in the coming days, while flows on several smaller rivers have fallen close to biological minimum levels after weeks of exceptionally dry weather.
Europe has been grappling with intense heatwave conditions and wildfires this season. Late in July, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) announced that over 434,000 hectares have already burned across Europe this year, according to the latest available data.
As wildfires continue to rage across Europe and North America, destroying forests, threatening communities and releasing vast amounts of carbon into the atmosphere, the 2026 fire season is once again demonstrating that while many fires cannot be stopped once they reach full intensity, much more can be done to prevent future disasters, said the UNECE.
